"Here are research options from several root questions, one per line as key: title. summary, where a key looks like R2:physical:W4. Group options that ask the same question of the same kind of system; every key goes in exactly one cluster, and a key that matches nothing is its own cluster. Name each cluster's topic in at least three words. Decide only from the text below; do not use tools.
R1:physical:K1: Single-chain MCMC mixing: the sequential autocorrelation bottleneck. A single Markov chain for a lumped conceptual model must run many serial iterations because posterior samples are autocorrelated; each step conditions on the previous state, and more parallel compute cannot shorten the chain's integrated autocorrelation time, only how fast samples accumulate.
R1:physical:K2: Ensemble / differential-evolution MCMC: running many chains in parallel. DREAM-style samplers run N chains simultaneously, generating each chain's proposal from differences of other chains' states; this improves exploration of multimodal/correlated hydrologic posteriors and enables Gelman–Rubin cross-chain diagnostics, and it is the one place where more GPUs change what gets sampled (by raising chain count) without lowering per-chain autocorrelation.
R1:physical:K3: Expensive distributed / high-dimensional forward models (MT-DREAM(ZS), MGB, SWAT). For spatially distributed models with hundreds-to-thousands of parameters the forward-model cost dominates the calibration budget, and the workload decomposes into thousands of independent model runs that are embarrassingly parallel across chains and parameter sets; here compute is a genuinely binding constraint that parallelism relieves.
R1:physical:K4: Large-sample multi-catchment calibration (CAMELS). Calibrating many catchments (CAMELS provides 671 US catchments) is embarrassingly parallel because each catchment is independently calibratable, so GPU/cloud throughput directly determines how many catchments get a proper Bayesian treatment rather than point optimization.
R1:interp:K1: Train sparse autoencoders on LSTM rainfall-runoff internals to expose representation-level equifinality. Apply Goodfire-style sparse autoencoders to LSTM cell-state activations to recover a sparse dictionary of hydrological features, then ask which features are uniquely constrained by the runoff record and which interchangeable feature sets reproduce it, reframing the framer's equifinality as non-identifiability of internal features.
R1:interp:K2: Steer SAE features of a differentiable rainfall-runoff model to separate identifiable from equifinal directions. Use Goodfire-style feature steering on a differentiable RR model (LSTM or autodiff GR4J) to measure which features causally change the simulated runoff and which do not, producing an intervention-based map of the posterior geometry that sets the autocorrelation time.
R1:interp:K3: Reparameterize the calibration with active subspaces to shorten the MCMC chain. Identify the few data-informed directions along which the forward model varies (the active subspace) and run MCMC only on those while sampling the prior elsewhere, the non-neural, interpretability-flavored cousin of feature extraction that directly attacks the autocorrelation time through reparameterization rather than hardware.

Return only one JSON value, with no other text, that matches this JSON Schema:
{\"type\":\"object\",\"properties\":{\"clusters\":{\"type\":\"array\",\"description\":\"Every option key in exactly one cluster; an option with no duplicate is a cluster of one.\",\"items\":{\"type\":\"object\",\"properties\":{\"topic\":{\"type\":\"string\",\"description\":\"What the members ask, in at least 3 words.\"},\"members\":{\"type\":\"array\",\"items\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"description\":\"Option keys.\"}},\"required\":[\"topic\",\"members\"]}}},\"required\":[\"clusters\"]}"

Let me analyze the options:

- R1:physical:K1: Single-chain MCMC mixing, autocorrelation bottleneck — serial autocorrelation time limitation.
- R1:physical:K2: Ensemble/DREAM MCMC parallel chains — more chains improve exploration, GPUs change sampling.
- R1:physical:K3: Expensive distributed forward models, embarrassingly parallel model runs, compute binding.
- R1:physical:K4: Large-sample multi-catchment calibration, embarrassingly parallel catchments.
- R1:interp:K1: SAE on LSTM internals, equifinality as non-identifiability.
- R1:interp:K2: Steer SAE features to separate identifiable/equifinal directions.
- R1:interp:K3: Active subspaces reparameterization to shorten MCMC chain.

Grouping "same question of same kind of system":

Cluster A: K2 and K3 and K4? Hmm. K2 is ensemble MCMC parallel chains for hydrologic calibration; K3 is expensive forward models parallel; K4 is large-sample catchments parallel. All are about "where does parallelism help hydrologic model calibration?" K3 and K4 are both "embarrassingly parallel" workload decomposition. K2 is about ensemble MCMC using parallel chains. They all ask: which parts of Bayesian hydrologic calibration benefit from parallel compute? Could group K2, K3, K4 together as "parallelism opportunities in hydrologic calibration". Alternatively, K3 and K4 together (embarrassingly parallel workloads) with K2 separate? But K2's summary also emphasizes parallel chains and GPUs helping. The question underlying all three: "where can more parallel compute improve hydrologic MCMC calibration?" I think grouping K2, K3, K4 is reasonable: "parallel compute's role in hydrologic calibration".

Alternatively K1 pairs with K3 (autocorrelation time vs cost)? K1 is a limitation: parallelism doesn't shorten autocorrelation. K2 contrasts: ensemble MCMC is where GPUs help. K1 and K2 are complementary but ask different questions: K1 asks why single chains can't be parallelized; K2 asks where parallel chains help. Hmm. The grouping criterion: "options that ask the same question of the same kind of system."

Possible clusters:
1. {K2, K3, K4}: "Where does parallelism accelerate hydrologic model calibration?" — same system (hydrologic MCMC calibration), same question (benefit of parallel compute).
2. {K1} alone: single-chain autocorrelation bottleneck — or group K1 with K2? K1 vs K2 seem like a contrast pair (parallelism doesn't help vs helps). But grouping them would conflate. I'd keep K1 own cluster: "limits of parallelism in single-chain MCMC" — but a cluster of one still needs a topic with ≥3 words.
3. {K1, interp K3}? K3 (interp) is about shortening the MCMC chain via reparameterization — attacks autocorrelation time, directly referencing K1's bottleneck. Question: "how to shorten MCMC autocorrelation time?" K1 states the bottleneck; interp K3 proposes a solution. Same kind of system? K1 is physical hydrologic models; interp K3 is non-neural but "interpretability-flavored". They both concern the autocorrelation time of hydrologic MCMC. Grouping K1 with R1:interp:K3 seems plausible: both about serial autocorrelation time of calibration MCMC. Hmm.

But the instruction: group options that ask the same question of the same kind of system. The keys have prefixes R1:physical and R1:interp, indicating two kinds of systems: physical hydrologic models vs interpretability of neural/differentiable models.

- interp K1 and interp K2 both use SAEs on differentiable rainfall-runoff models to study equifinality/identifiability. Clearly a cluster: "SAE-based equifinality analysis of rainfall-runoff models."
- interp K3 is about active subspaces reparameterization to shorten MCMC chain — different question (MCMC efficiency) though interpretability-flavored. Could be its own cluster, or grouped with physical K1.

Physical K1: single-chain MCMC autocorrelation bottleneck. interp K3: reparameterize to shorten chain (attack autocorrelation time). Both ask "how to deal with / what determines MCMC autocorrelation time?" Same question? K1 asks why the chain is long (diagnosis); K3 asks how to shorten it (remedy). They address the autocorrelation bottleneck. Same kind of system? K1 is lumped conceptual model; K3 is a differentiable RR model (autodiff GR4J) or generally calibration. Hmm, K3 says "the non-neural, interpretability-flavored cousin of feature extraction that directly attacks the autocorrelation time." So K3 explicitly links to K1's bottleneck.

I think reasonable clustering:

Cluster 1: R1:physical:K2, R1:physical:K3, R1:physical:K4 — "Where parallel compute helps hydrologic calibration" (ensemble chains, embarrassingly parallel forward runs, many catchments).

Cluster 2: R1:physical:K1 and R1:interp:K3 — "Shortening MCMC autocorrelation time in calibration" — K1 identifies the serial bottleneck; K3 attacks it via reparameterization. Both about the autocorrelation time of hydrologic MCMC.

Cluster 3: R1:interp:K1, R1:interp:K2 — "SAE analysis of equifinality in differentiable rainfall-runoff models."

Alternatively Cluster 2 could be just K1 alone, with interp K3 alone. But the question says "Group options that ask the same question of the same kind of system." K1 and interp K3 both ask about the autocorrelation-time bottleneck of MCMC for hydrologic calibration — I'd say same question ("what determines / how to reduce MCMC autocorrelation in hydrologic calibration?"). Kinds of systems: lumped conceptual model vs differentiable model — hmm, not identical, but K3 explicitly targets the same autocorrelation time. The grouping seems more informative and defensible than leaving them separate.

Actually, let me reconsider: maybe the intended grouping is by the framer's structure: physical K1–K4 are all about MCMC parallelism in hydrology; interp K1–K3 about interpretability. But the task says group same question + same kind of system.

K1's question: "Why can't parallel compute shorten a single MCMC chain?" — a limitation statement.
K2's question: "Where do parallel chains/GPUs help sampling?" — K1 and K2 are a contrast but different questions.

Hmm. Another plausible grouping: K1 alone ("serial autocorrelation limits of single-chain MCMC"), K2+K3+K4 together ("where parallelism aids hydrologic Bayesian calibration"), interp K1+K2 together, interp K3 alone ("reparameterization to shorten MCMC chains via active subspaces"). That yields K3(interp) as its own cluster. That's also fine.

Which is better? The criterion "same question of the same kind of system." interp K3 is explicitly "non-neural" — the system is a hydrologic calibration (GR4J), same as physical ones. Its question: how to shorten autocorrelation time via reparameterization. K1's question: the chain must run many serial iterations because samples are autocorrelated — the question could be framed as "does parallel compute help single-chain MCMC?" Answer: no, due to autocorrelation. interp K3 attacks the autocorrelation time through reparameterization. Both revolve around the integrated autocorrelation time of hydrologic MCMC. I'll group them: topic "Reducing MCMC autocorrelation time in hydrologic calibration" — that's ≥3 words.

Hmm, but is K1 asking the same question as K3? K1 diagnoses; K3 fixes. The shared question: "what sets the MCMC autocorrelation time and can it be reduced without hardware?" Actually K2's summary also mentions "without lowering per-chain autocorrelation" — K2 notes GPUs raise chain count without lowering per-chain autocorrelation. So autocorrelation time threads through K1, K2, K3(interp).

I think a defensible, clean output:

Cluster 1: K1(physical) + K3(interp): "Attacking the serial autocorrelation bottleneck in hydrologic MCMC" — members ["R1:physical:K1","R1:interp:K3"].

Wait, but K1 is more "bottleneck exists, parallelism can't help" while K3(interp) is "reparameterize to shorten chain." Both about autocorrelation time. I'll go with grouping them since they directly reference each other's concern (K3 says "directly attacks the autocorrelation time").

Hmm, but "same kind of system": K1 = lumped conceptual hydrologic model; K3 = differentiable RR model / active subspaces on forward model. Both are hydrologic forward-model calibrations, non-neural in K3's case ("non-neural... cousin"). K1's system is also non-neural. So yes, same kind of system: hydrologic conceptual/differentiable model calibration. Good.

Cluster 2: K2, K3, K4 physical: "Where parallel compute accelerates hydrologic Bayesian calibration" — ensemble parallel chains, embarrassingly parallel forward runs, many catchments. All about exploiting parallelism in hydrologic calibration.

Cluster 3: interp K1, K2: "SAE feature analysis of equifinality in differentiable rainfall-runoff models."

That covers all 7 keys: physical K1,K2,K3,K4; interp K1,K2,K3. Every key exactly once.

Topic names ≥3 words:
1. "Serial autocorrelation bottleneck of hydrologic MCMC calibration" — or "Shortening MCMC autocorrelation time via reparameterization". Let me phrase: "Reducing serial autocorrelation in hydrologic MCMC".
2. "Exploiting parallel compute in hydrologic calibration".
3. "SAE-based equifinality analysis of rainfall-runoff models".

Output JSON only.
